g.text: The per-recipient STATE multiplies. The content does not.
40 billion recipient copies a day come from 10 billion emails - a 4x amplification, and separating the two is worth 548 PB a year.
One send, four inboxes - and one stored body
sender
one email
to: 4 recipients
content-addressed store IMMUTABLE, stored ONCE
sha256(body) -> one blob
sha256(attachment) -> one blob
user 1 is_read folder labels -> body_hash
user 2 is_read folder labels -> body_hash
user 3 is_read folder labels -> body_hash
user 4 is_read folder labels -> body_hash
x 4
A message to four people has
ONE body and FOUR sets of
per-recipient state - each of
which can independently mark
it read, move it, label it or
delete it.
Which also means marking an
email read is a tiny row
update rather than touching a
50 KB blob.
The dashed lines are pointers,
not copies. Attachment dedup
extends further than 4x: the
same slide deck forwarded
around a company is stored
once regardless of how many
separate emails carry it - and
a content hash is an obvious
key, because attachments are
immutable by nature.
The same question, two very different answers
bodies, full copy per recipient
2.0 PB / day 730 PB / year
bodies, content-addressed
0.50 PB / day 182 PB / year
attachments, per recipient
4.0 PB / day 1,460 PB / year
attachments, deduplicated by hash
1.0 PB / day 365 PB / year
1B users x 10 sent/day = 10 BILLION emails sent/day (~116,000 sends/sec), and 1B x 40 received = 40 BILLION recipient copies.
The metadata itself is small by comparison - 40 billion rows/day at ~500 bytes is 20 TB/day - but it is the part that must be
QUERYABLE, which is why the schema separates it from the content entirely.
Email is a federated protocol, not a product - so you do not control both ends
A message leaves your servers and arrives at Gmail, at Outlook, or at a Postfix box somebody runs in their basement, over SMTP
- a protocol from 1982. You cannot change it, cannot version it, and cannot assume the other side is well-behaved. Whole
sections of this design exist because of that, and it is what makes email unlike a chat system.
protocol
purpose
who uses it here
SMTP
server-to-server transfer, and client submission
MANDATORY - this is how mail reaches other providers
POP3
client downloads mail, then it is DELETED from the server
legacy; supported for old clients
IMAP
client reads mail, kept server-side, with folder sync
legacy; supported for old clients
HTTPS
not an email protocol at all
THE PRIMARY CLIENT API
SMTP is non-negotiable - it is the federation layer. But for YOUR OWN clients, HTTP wins on extensibility: IMAP's command set
is fixed and ancient, with no vocabulary for labels-instead-of-folders, snooze, conversation threading, server-side smart
categorization, or push to a browser. Every one of those would need a protocol extension no client supports. A REST/JSON API
over HTTPS lets the product evolve, works in a browser, and pairs naturally with WebSocket for push.
The cost is real and worth stating: you must STILL implement IMAP and POP3 for users with existing mail clients, so you end up
maintaining three client protocols instead of one. A deliberate trade - pay for legacy support, do not let it constrain the
product.
Four ideas - and the first two come straight from the arithmetic
1 separate content from per-recipient state
the body and attachments are stored once, content-
addressed; each recipient gets a small metadata row
pointing at them, carrying their own read flag, folder
and labels. The 4x storage win.
2 partition everything by user_id
almost every operation - fetch a folder, mark read,
search, delete - is scoped to ONE user and never spans
users. So every operation is single-partition with no
cross-node coordination. The cost: a shared mailbox
genuinely owned by several users does not fit, and this
design accepts that rather than paying for it.
3 accept the mail, THEN process it
inbound SMTP is acknowledged as soon as the message is
durably queued; spam checks, indexing and fan-out
happen asynchronously. Under SMTP, accepting a message
means TAKING RESPONSIBILITY for it - so the queue write
must be durable BEFORE the acknowledgement, and
everything after can be retried.
4 treat deliverability as an engineering problem
standing up an SMTP server is trivial; getting mail into
an inbox rather than a spam folder is a months-long
reputation exercise - dedicated IPs, gradual warm-up,
SPF/DKIM/DMARC, feedback loops with the large providers.
An interviewer asking 'how do you build Gmail' is asking
about this whether they know it or not.
The search index is write-heavy and read-LIGHT - the opposite of every other search system
index writes
40 BILLION / day, matching the metadata rate
search queries
a handful per user per WEEK
That single fact drives the engine choice, and it is the most commonly missed point about email search: an index optimized for
query latency at the cost of write amplification is exactly the wrong trade here.
Three API details that carry real weight
202 Accepted for sending, not 200 OK
the system has taken the message and will ATTEMPT
delivery; it cannot promise the recipient's server
will accept it. Delivery may take seconds or, with
retries against an unavailable destination, days.
Reporting 200 would claim a guarantee SMTP
fundamentally cannot provide - and a bounce arriving
four hours later is a normal outcome, not an error.
attachments upload separately and return a content_hash
two reasons: a 25 MB upload should not block
composing, and the hash is what enables the dedup
worth 1 PB/day. A client re-attaching a file the
server already has can skip the upload entirely.
folder listing returns HEADERS ONLY
a folder view shows sender, subject, date and read
state - not bodies. Bodies are ~50 KB and headers a
few hundred bytes, so fetching 50 full messages to
render a list would be ~2.5 MB for a screen that
displays a few kilobytes. Which is why headers and
bodies live in different places.
